newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Trade in Automakers to be probed-sources.
newsitem.headline: Trade in Automakers to be probed-sources.

text.p: South Africa's Securities Regulation Panel will probe recent trade in carmaker Automakers Ltd stock following its rapid rise ahead of an announcement on a tie-up with a foreign firm, industry sources said on Monday.
"We have a duty to investigate what might appear to be insider trading," a panel source told Reuters.
The panel's executive director, Richard Connellan, said he could not confirm that an investigation was taking place.
"We can't give any comment on that," he said.
The regulation panel is a statutory body independent of the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE), but they usually work closely together on investigations.
A JSE source confirmed the two had discussed the trade in Automakers shares and were looking into the matter.
The firm's stock began to jump on Thursday, when it rose 76 cents to 2.80 rand. Automakers then issued a terse cautionary statement urging shareholders not to trade their stock.
The rise continued on Friday as dealers identified Japan's Nissan and Italy's Fiat as companies which might be poised to take a stake in the firm.
On Monday Automakers issued a notice confirming it would delist in a move to bring in a still unidentified minority shareholder. The firm's stock rose to 380 cents, up 50 cents by 0917 GMT.
Minority shareholders will get 411 cents a share as part of the deal and the buyout price represents a 76 percent premium to the average closing price of the share over the last 20 days.

Under the scheme, Automakers' majority shareholder Sankorp -- which holds 50.7 percent of the issued share capital -- will make the payout to minorities ahead of bringing in the international concern.
Fiat has denied any interest in Automakers while Nissan declined comment, leaving the Japanese company as firm favourite in the minds of many market players.
Automakers spokesman Johan Kleynhans said he could not confirm the company was in talks with Nissan.
He added that as far as he knew the company had not been contacted by the stock exchange or regulation panel about possible leaks of price sensitive information on the deal.
